title: Light — Reflection and Refraction
short: Ray diagrams, mirror and lens formulas, magnification and power.
lede: Six standard ray diagrams unlock every numerical in this chapter. Learn the sign convention once and the rest is substitution.
lens: **3–4 marks.** One ray diagram, one numerical on the mirror or lens formula, and one question on magnification or power.
Case-based questions give a practical situation — a dentist's mirror, a vehicle's rear-view mirror, a torch reflector — and ask which mirror is used and why.
concepts: **1. Reflection.** Light travelling in a straight line bounces back on striking a polished surface. **Laws of reflection:** the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. A **plane mirror** always forms a virtual, erect image, the same size as the object, at the same distance behind the mirror, and laterally inverted.

**2. Spherical mirrors.** **Concave** (converging, reflecting surface curves inwards) and **convex** (diverging). Key points: **P** (pole), **C** (centre of curvature), **F** (principal focus, midway between P and C), **R = 2f**. Aperture is the diameter of the reflecting surface.

concepts: **3. Refraction.** The bending of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium into another, caused by the change in its speed. Light bends **toward** the normal going from a rarer to a denser medium and **away** from the normal going the other way. It does not bend when it strikes the surface normally. Laws: (i) the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; (ii) **Snell's law** — the ratio sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media; this constant is the **refractive index**.

**4. Refractive index.** `n = c/v` (speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in the medium); it has no unit. Relative refractive index `n21 = n2/n1 = v1/v2`. Air ≈ 1.0003, water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.42 — diamond's high value gives it brilliance through total internal reflection.

**5. Lenses.** **Convex** (converging, thicker at the centre) and **concave** (diverging). A convex lens forms a real, inverted image for objects beyond F, and a **virtual, erect, magnified** image when the object is between F and the optical centre (this is why it is used as a magnifying glass). A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image.

**6. Power.** `P = 1/f` where f is in **metres**; the unit is the **dioptre (D)**. Convex lens power is positive, concave lens power negative. Powers of lenses in contact add up: `P = P1 + P2 + P3`. Prescriptions read +2.0 D (convex, for hypermetropia) or −1.5 D (concave, for myopia).

Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
R = 2f
Magnification m = h'/h = −v/u  (mirror)   and  m = h'/h = v/u  (lens)
Power P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre (D)
tricks: - **Sign convention:** distances measured against the direction of the incident light (to the left of the pole) are negative. Object distance **u is always negative**. For a concave mirror **f is negative**; for a convex mirror and a convex lens **f is positive**; a concave lens has negative f.
- **Nature from the sign of v:** for a mirror, negative v = real image (in front); positive v = virtual (behind). For a lens, positive v = real (on the other side); negative v = virtual (same side).
- **'Convex mirror = always virtual, erect, diminished'** — the reason it is used as a rear-view mirror, giving a wider field of view.
mistakes: - Using the mirror formula for a lens. Lens formula has **−v** and **+u** in the same form: `1/v − 1/u = 1/f`.
- Forgetting to convert f from cm to m before computing power. f = 20 cm must be written as **0.2 m**.
- Dropping the negative sign of m for a real, inverted image.
- Drawing the ray diagram without arrowheads on the rays and without marking C, F and P.

qa.q: State the mirror formula and the SI unit of the power of a lens.
qa.a: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. The SI unit of power is the **dioptre (D)**, equal to 1 m⁻¹.

qa.q: Why is a convex mirror preferred as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
qa.a: Because it always gives an erect, virtual and diminished image, and it has a wider field of view than a plane mirror, so the driver can see a much larger area of the traffic behind.

qa.q: A lens of power −4.0 D is placed in the path of light. Find its focal length and identify it.
qa.a: P = 1/f, so f = 1/(−4.0) = −0.25 m = −25 cm. Negative focal length means it is a **concave (diverging) lens**.

qa.q: Define the principal focus of a concave mirror and relate it to the radius of curvature.
qa.a: The principal focus is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (or appear to meet) after reflection. For a spherical mirror the focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature, so f = R/2.

qa.q: An object 4 cm high is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image.
a: So **v = −37.5 cm** — the image forms 37.5 cm in front of the mirror, hence real and inverted.
m = −v/u = −(−37.5)/(−25) = −1.5, so h' = −1.5 × 4 = **−6 cm**: the image is 6 cm tall, inverted, and magnified.

qa.q: Draw a ray diagram for an object placed between C and F of a concave mirror and state the nature of the image.
a: Draw the principal axis with P, F and C marked. Place the object (an arrow) between C and F.
Ray 1: parallel to the axis, reflected through F. Ray 2: through F, reflected parallel to the axis. (A third ray through C retraces its path.)
The rays meet **beyond C**, so the image is **real, inverted and magnified**. This is the arrangement used in a shaving or makeup mirror when the object is close.

qa.q: State the sign convention used for spherical mirrors and lenses, and apply it to a concave mirror.
a: All distances are measured from the pole (mirror) or the optical centre (lens).
Distances measured in the direction of the incident light are positive and those against it are negative; heights above the principal axis are positive and those below are negative.

qa.q: State the laws of refraction and solve: light enters from air into glass (n = 1.5) with an angle of incidence of 30°. Find the angle of refraction and the speed of light in glass.

**Angle of refraction:** sin r = sin i / n = 0.5/1.5 = 0.3333, so r ≈ **19.5°** — the ray bends toward the normal.

title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
short: Defects of vision, dispersion, atmospheric refraction and scattering.
lede: Four defects, four corrections, and four sky-colour reasons. Small chapter, guaranteed marks.
lens: **2–3 marks.** Myopia/hypermetropia with a labelled diagram is the single most repeated question in Physics.
The 'why is the sky blue / why is the sunrise red' question appears regularly as a 2-mark reasoning item.
concepts: **1. The eye as a camera.** **Cornea** — most of the refraction happens here. **Iris** — the dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the **pupil** and hence the amount of light entering. **Crystalline lens** — a convex lens of adjustable focal length; **ciliary muscles** change its curvature, so a clear image is formed on the **retina** for objects at all distances. This is the **power of accommodation**. The image on the retina is real and inverted; the optic nerve carries the signal to the brain. The **blind spot** is where the optic nerve leaves and there are no photoreceptors. **Least distance of distinct vision** = 25 cm for a normal adult eye; far point = infinity.

**2. Defects of vision.** **Myopia** (short sight) — the person sees near objects clearly but not distant ones; caused by excessive curvature of the lens or elongation of the eyeball; the image forms **in front of** the retina; corrected with a **concave lens**. **Hypermetropia** (long sight) — cannot see nearby objects clearly; image forms **behind** the retina; corrected with a **convex lens**. **Presbyopia** — the power of accommodation decreases with age; corrected with a **bifocal lens**.

**3. Dispersion.** The splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours (VIBGYOR) by a glass prism. Newton showed with two identical prisms, one inverted over the other, that white light is a mixture of colours. Red bends least, violet most, because different colours travel at different speeds in glass. **Rainbow formation:** refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection of sunlight by water droplets acting as tiny prisms — you see it with the sun behind you.

**4. Atmospheric refraction.** The refractive index of air decreases with altitude, so light from a star bends continuously as it enters the atmosphere. Effects: **stars twinkle** (the apparent position and brightness keep changing), **planets do not twinkle** (they are nearer and act as extended sources, so the variations average out), the **sun appears above the horizon about two minutes before actual sunrise and two minutes after sunset** (daylight is lengthened by about 4 minutes), and **stars appear slightly higher** than their true position.

**5. Scattering of light.** Fine particles scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths more strongly — the **Tyndall effect**. This explains the **blue colour of the sky**, the **reddish appearance of the sun at sunrise and sunset** (blue is scattered away over the long path, leaving red), the **white appearance of clouds** (large water droplets scatter all colours equally), and why **danger signals are red** (red scatters least and travels farthest through fog and smoke). At noon the sun looks white because the path through the atmosphere is short.
formulas: Power of a lens: P = 1/f (f in metres, P in dioptres)
Correction: myopia → concave (diverging) lens of negative power; hypermetropia → convex (converging) lens of positive power
Presbyopia → bifocal lens; astigmatism → cylindrical lens
Scattering intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ — shorter wavelength scatters far more
Refractive index and deviation: violet deviates most, red least
tricks: - **Myopia = image in front = concave lens.** *'My-o-pia → My oh, I can't see far → Concave.'*
- **Hypermetropia = image behind = convex lens.** *'Hyper → beyond → behind → convex.'*
- **VIBGYOR: red deviates least, violet most.** Same order explains the rainbow and the prism.
mistakes: - Drawing the corrective lens on the wrong side of the eye diagram, or labelling the image position incorrectly (in front for myopia, behind for hypermetropia).
- Saying 'the sky is blue because it reflects the sea'. It is **scattering** by air molecules.
- Explaining twinkling as 'stars burning unevenly'. It is **atmospheric refraction**.
- Forgetting that **presbyopia** is due to the weakening of the ciliary muscles and loss of flexibility of the lens, not a change in the eyeball's length.

qa.q: Name the part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering it, and the least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye.
qa.a: The iris (which adjusts the size of the pupil); 25 cm.

qa.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets do not?
qa.a: Starlight passes through layers of air of changing refractive index, so its path keeps changing slightly and the apparent brightness and position fluctuate — the star twinkles. Planets are much nearer and behave as a collection of many point sources, so the fluctuations from different parts cancel out and the total light remains steady.

qa.q: Why does the sun appear reddish early in the morning?
qa.a: Because near the horizon sunlight travels through a much thicker layer of air. The shorter blue wavelengths are scattered away, and mainly the longer red wavelengths reach our eyes, so the sun looks red. At noon the path is short, little blue light is scattered, and the sun looks white.

qa.q: What is the power of accommodation of the eye?
qa.a: It is the ability of the eye lens to change its focal length — by the action of the ciliary muscles — so that both near and distant objects are focused sharply on the retina. In a normal eye the near point is about 25 cm and the far point is infinity.

qa.q: What is myopia? State its two causes and its correction.
a: Myopia (short-sightedness) is the defect in which a person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly; the image of a distant object forms **in front of the retina**.
**Causes:** (i) excessive curvature of the eye lens, (ii) elongation of the eyeball.
**Correction:** a **concave lens** of suitable power, which diverges the light so that the image is formed exactly on the retina.

qa.q: Explain the formation of a rainbow in the sky.
a: After rain, tiny water droplets remain suspended in the air and act as small glass prisms.

Sunlight entering a droplet is first **refracted and dispersed** into its constituent colours, then undergoes **total internal reflection** at the inner surface of the droplet, and is **refracted again** as it leaves.
Because different colours emerge at slightly different angles, the observer sees a coloured arc — a rainbow — with the sun always behind them.

qa.q: What is presbyopia? State its cause and how it is corrected.
a: Presbyopia is the loss of the eye's power of accommodation with age: the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible.
As a result the near point recedes and reading or threading a needle becomes difficult.
It is corrected with converging (convex) spectacles; when a person has both myopia and presbyopia, bifocal lenses are used.

qa.q: Explain why the sky looks blue and the sun looks white at noon but red at sunrise.
a: Air molecules and fine particles scatter light of short wavelength much more strongly than long wavelength light (scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴).
Blue light is scattered the most, so light reaching the eye from all parts of the sky is rich in blue.
At noon the sun is overhead and its light crosses the shortest possible path, so very little blue is removed and the sun looks white.
Near sunrise and sunset the path through the atmosphere is much longer, most of the blue is scattered away, and the remaining direct light looks red.

qa.q: Explain atmospheric refraction and describe any three phenomena based on it.
a: **Atmospheric refraction** is the bending of light as it passes through layers of air of different densities; the refractive index of air decreases as we go up, so light from a celestial body bends gradually toward the normal.
**(1) Twinkling of stars:** the continuously changing refractive index makes the apparent position and brightness of a star fluctuate.

**(2) Advance of sunrise and delay of sunset:** light from the sun below the horizon is refracted toward the earth, so the sun becomes visible about two minutes before actual sunrise and remains visible about two minutes after sunset — the day is lengthened by about 4 minutes.
**(3) Apparent flattening of the sun's disc** at sunrise and sunset, and stars appearing slightly higher than their true position, are also caused by the same refraction.

title: Electricity
short: Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, heating effect and power.
lede: The most numerical-heavy chapter in the paper. Three formulas cover everything; the rest is careful reading of the circuit.
lens: **3–4 marks.** A series or parallel circuit numerical is almost certain, plus one question on the heating effect or on power rating.
Case-based questions usually give a household circuit (parallel wiring) and ask why appliances are connected in parallel and what happens to the resistance.
concepts: **1. Electric current and potential difference.** Current `I = Q/t`, measured in **amperes** with an **ammeter** connected **in series**. Potential difference `V = W/Q`, measured in **volts** with a **voltmeter** connected **in parallel**; 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. By convention current flows from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to the flow of electrons. A **cell** maintains the potential difference that drives the charge.

**2. Ohm's law.** At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends: `V = IR`. The **V–I graph** for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; its slope gives R. Resistance is the property that opposes the flow of current, `R = ρl/A`, measured in **ohms (Ω)** — it increases with length, decreases with area of cross-section, and depends on the material and temperature.

**3. Resistors in series.** The same current flows through each; total `R = R1 + R2 + R3`, which is **greater than the largest** individual resistance. Voltages divide in the ratio of the resistances. Series wiring is used when the total resistance must be increased, as in a decorative bulb string.

**4. Resistors in parallel.** The same potential difference is across each; `1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3`, and the total is **less than the smallest** individual resistance. This is why domestic appliances are connected in parallel — each gets the full supply voltage, each has its own switch, and the failure of one does not affect the others.

**5. Heating effect of current.** `H = I²Rt` (joules) — also written `H = VIt = V²t/R`. Applications: the **electric heater, geyser and iron** (high-resistance nichrome heating element), the **electric bulb** (tungsten filament, melting point 3380 °C, filled with argon and nitrogen so the filament does not oxidise), and the **electric fuse** (a wire of low melting point in series that melts if the current exceeds a safe value; ISI mark and rating such as 5 A). A **circuit breaker** and **earthing** (the metal body of an appliance connected to the earth) protect the user from electric shock.
formulas: I = Q/t ; 1 A = 1 C/s
V = W/Q ; 1 V = 1 J/C
V = IR ; R = ρl/A
Series: Rs = R1 + R2 + R3
Parallel: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3
H = I²Rt = VIt = V²t/R
P = VI = I²R = V²/R ; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
tricks: - **Series = same current, voltage divides. Parallel = same voltage, current divides.** Read that sentence before every circuit question.
- **Parallel resistance is always smaller** than the smallest resistor. If your answer is bigger, you have used the series formula.
- **Units for energy:** the board wants kWh for a household bill. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Always convert hours, not minutes.

- Using `H = I²Rt` and then quoting the answer in kWh without converting joules.

title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
short: Field patterns, the three hand rules, the motor and the generator.
lede: Rule-heavy but very short. Get Fleming's two rules and the three hand rules straight and the questions are mechanical.
lens: **2–3 marks.** Fleming's left-hand and right-hand rules and the difference between AC and DC are asked repeatedly.
Domestic circuits and the role of the earth wire or fuse are a favourite case-based topic.
concepts: **1. Magnetic field and field lines.** A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet in which its force can be detected. Field lines are **closed continuous curves** — outside a bar magnet they run from the **north to the south pole** and inside from south to north. Two field lines never intersect (that would mean two directions of force at one point). The relative strength is shown by how close the lines are.

**2. Field around a current-carrying conductor.** A straight wire produces **concentric circles** around it; increasing the current or decreasing the distance from the wire strengthens the field. A circular loop produces concentric circles that are nearly parallel at the centre; a **solenoid** produces a field like a bar magnet, with one end behaving as the north pole — this is how an **electromagnet** is made. **Oersted's experiment** showed that a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire is deflected, so an electric current produces a magnetic field.

**3. Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.** A conductor carrying current placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is **maximum when the conductor is perpendicular** to the field. **Fleming's left-hand rule:** stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; if the **forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field** and the **middle finger in the direction of the current**, then the **thumb gives the direction of the force** (motion). This is the principle of the **electric motor**.

**4. The electric motor.** A rectangular coil placed between the poles of a magnet; when current flows, the coil experiences a torque and rotates. The **split ring (commutator)** reverses the direction of current in the coil every half rotation, so the rotation continues in one direction. Uses: fans, mixers, washing machines, pumps. **Electromagnetic induction:** when the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a current is induced in it — **Fleming's right-hand rule** gives the direction of the induced current (thumb = motion, forefinger = field, middle finger = induced current).

**5. The electric generator.** It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. A **DC generator** uses a split-ring commutator and gives current in one direction; an **AC generator** uses two slip rings and the current reverses direction periodically. In India, AC has a frequency of **50 Hz**, so its direction changes **100 times in one second**.

**6. Domestic electric circuits.** Live wire (red, 220 V), neutral (black, 0 V) and earth wire (green, connected to a metal plate deep in the earth). Appliances with metallic bodies — geysers, irons, toasters — are earthed so that leakage current flows to the earth instead of through the user. **Short circuit** — live and neutral touch, resistance becomes almost zero, current rises enormously. **Overloading** — too many appliances on one circuit. **Fuse** and **MCB** protect the circuit; separate circuits of 15 A and 5 A are provided.
formulas: Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = B I L (for a conductor perpendicular to the field)
Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field, Second finger = Current, Thumb = Force (motion)
Fleming's right-hand rule: for induced current in a generator
Domestic supply in India: 220 V, 50 Hz AC — live (red/brown), neutral (black/blue), earth (green)
Fuse rating: choose a fuse whose rating is just above the current the appliance draws
tricks: - **Left hand = Motor, Right hand = Generator.** *'M' for motor and 'M' is in the word 'Motion' — but remember: the **left** hand has the thumb as Force, so Motor = Left.*
- **Field lines never intersect** — the standard one-mark reason question.
- **AC 50 Hz changes direction 100 times a second** (twice per cycle).
mistakes: - Saying field lines run from south to north *outside* a magnet. Outside it is **north to south**.
- Mixing up Fleming's left-hand rule (force/motor) with the right-hand rule (induced current/generator).
- Stating that the split ring makes the motor faster. It **reverses the current** every half rotation so that rotation continues in one direction.
- Forgetting that the earth wire is connected to the **metallic body** of the appliance, not to the live wire.

qa.q: State Fleming's right-hand rule.
qa.a: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the thumb in the direction of motion of the conductor, the middle finger gives the direction of the induced current.

qa.q: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect each other?
qa.a: Because at the point of intersection there would be two directions of the magnetic field for a single point, which is impossible — a compass needle placed there could not point in two directions at once.

qa.q: Differentiate between an AC generator and a DC generator.
qa.a: An **AC generator** uses two complete slip rings, and the current it produces reverses direction periodically (50 Hz in India). A **DC generator** uses a split-ring commutator, so although the current in the coil reverses, the current in the external circuit always flows in one direction.

qa.q: State the rule used to find the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
qa.a: Right-hand thumb rule: imagine holding the conductor in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the current; the direction in which your fingers curl around the conductor is the direction of the magnetic field lines, which are concentric circles around the wire.

qa.q: Explain the principle and working of an electric motor.
a: **Principle:** a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
**Working:** a rectangular coil ABCD is placed between the poles of a magnet. When current flows, one arm is pushed up and the other down, so the coil rotates.
The **split-ring commutator** reverses the direction of current in the coil after every half rotation, so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.
**Uses:** electric fans, mixers, washing machines and pumps.

qa.q: What is electromagnetic induction? Describe an activity to demonstrate it.
a: When the magnetic field linked with a coil changes, a current is induced in the coil — this is electromagnetic induction.

**Activity:** connect a galvanometer to a coil. Push a bar magnet's north pole into the coil and the galvanometer needle deflects momentarily in one direction; pull it out and it deflects in the opposite direction; hold it still inside and there is no deflection.
The deflection shows that a current is induced only when the magnetic flux through the coil is changing, i.e. only while the magnet is in relative motion.

task: Build a simple electromagnet: wind 40 turns of insulated copper wire around an iron nail, connect it to two cells in series with a switch, and test how many pins it picks up. steps: 1. Apply **Maxwell's right-hand thumb rule** to fix the direction of the field: thumb along the current, fingers curl along the field lines.
2. For the force on a conductor, use **Fleming's left-hand rule** (left hand for the motor effect): first finger field, second finger current, thumb force — all three mutually perpendicular.
3. For an induced current, switch to **Fleming's right-hand rule** (right hand for the generator effect) and state Faraday's law: the induced current is largest when the magnet or coil moves fast.

4. Finish with the **device and its safety part** — an electric motor uses a commutator to reverse current every half turn; domestic circuits use a fuse or MCB in the live wire, and earthing on the metal body of the appliance.

title: Our Environment
short: Food chains, the 10% law, ozone depletion and waste management.
lede: Five marks for an afternoon of study. The best marks-per-hour in the whole paper — do not leave it to the last day.
lens: **3–5 marks.** A food-chain question with the 10% energy calculation, one on ozone depletion, and one on biodegradable waste or the two environmental problems.
Case-based questions give a food chain with an energy value at one level and ask you to work out the others.
concepts: **1. Ecosystem.** All the living organisms (**biotic**) in an area together with the non-living (**abiotic**) components — temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals — form an ecosystem. **Producers** (green plants and blue-green algae) make their own food; **consumers** depend on them (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, parasites); **decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil. A pond and a forest are natural ecosystems; a crop field and an aquarium are artificial ones.

**2. Food chain and trophic levels.** A **food chain** shows who eats whom for the transfer of food energy: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk. Each step is a **trophic level**; producers occupy the first level. Energy flow in a food chain is always **unidirectional** — it passes from one level to the next and is never returned to the sun. A **food web** is a network of interconnected food chains.

**3. The 10% law.** Only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the remaining 90% is lost as heat, used in metabolism, or left in undigested matter. So if producers have 10,000 J, the herbivore gets 1,000 J, the next level 100 J, and the top carnivore only 10 J. This is why food chains rarely have more than four levels, and why a vegetarian diet supports a larger population.

**4. Biological magnification.** Harmful chemicals such as DDT and mercury are non-biodegradable and accumulate at **each** trophic level, so their concentration is **maximum in the top carnivore** — including human beings, who sit at the top of many food chains.

**5. Ozone layer depletion.** Ozone (O3) in the upper atmosphere shields the earth from harmful **ultraviolet radiation**. **Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**, used in refrigerators and air conditioners and in fire extinguishers, destroy ozone molecules, thinning the layer. Increased UV causes **skin cancer** and damage to crops and marine life. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** froze CFC production at 1986 levels to protect the ozone layer.

**6. Waste management.** **Biodegradable** waste (paper, vegetable peels, wood) is broken down by decomposers; **non-biodegradable** waste (plastic, glass, DDT, aluminium) is not. Problems caused by non-biodegradable waste: it does not decompose, pollutes soil and water, blocks drainage, and can enter food chains and biomagnify. Even biodegradable waste in excess causes foul smell, breeds mosquitoes and disease, and produces gases. **Methods of disposal:** segregating waste, **recycling** (paper, plastic, glass, metal), **composting and vermicomposting**, **sewage treatment** before releasing water into rivers, and burying waste in sanitary landfills. The **5 R's**: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle.
formulas: Energy at level n+1 = 10% of energy at level n
O3 formation: O2 + O →(UV) O3 ;  O3 + CFC → destruction of ozone
tricks: - **10% calculation:** move the decimal one place to the left at each level going up, and one place to the right going down.
- **Biomagnification = maximum at the top.** If the question asks which organism has the highest concentration, pick the top carnivore.
- **Biodegradable vs non-biodegradable** is decided by whether **micro-organisms can break it down** — not by whether it looks natural.
mistakes: - Drawing arrows in a food chain from predator to prey. Arrows always point **toward** the organism that eats — i.e. in the direction of **energy flow**.
- Applying 10% in the wrong direction. Going **down** the chain, multiply by 10 at each step, not by 0.1.
- Saying the ozone layer protects us from infrared radiation. It is **ultraviolet** radiation.
- Confusing **biological magnification** with **biodegradability** — they are different concepts entirely.

qa.q: Name the organisms that always occupy the first trophic level of a food chain, and define an ecosystem.
qa.a: Green plants and blue-green algae (producers). An ecosystem is a self-sustaining system in which all the living organisms of an area interact with each other and with the non-living (abiotic) components such as soil, water and air.

qa.q: Why are some substances biodegradable and some non-biodegradable?
qa.a: Because micro-organisms such as bacteria and fungi produce enzymes that can break down only certain substances like paper, wood and vegetable waste. Substances such as plastic, glass and DDT cannot be acted upon by these enzymes, so they remain in the environment for a very long time and are called non-biodegradable.

qa.q: Suggest two ways to reduce the problem of waste disposal.
qa.a: Segregate waste at the source and send biodegradable waste for composting or vermicomposting; and practise the 5 R's — refuse what is unnecessary, reduce consumption, reuse containers, repurpose items, and recycle paper, plastic, glass and metal.

qa.q: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web.
qa.a: A food chain is a single linear sequence showing who eats whom, for example grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. A food web is a network of many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem; because each organism can feed at more than one level, the web is far more stable than a single chain.

qa.q: In a food chain, if 10,000 joules of solar energy is available to the producers, how much energy will be available to the secondary consumer?
a: Producers convert about 1% of the solar energy into food energy, but taking 10,000 J as the energy **in the producers**: primary consumer receives 10% = **1,000 J**.
Secondary consumer receives 10% of 1,000 J = **100 J**.

qa.q: What is ozone? How is it formed, and why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern?
a: Ozone is a molecule of oxygen with three atoms, O3, found in the upper atmosphere.
**Formation:** ultraviolet radiation splits an oxygen molecule into free oxygen atoms, O2 →(UV) 2O; each free atom combines with an oxygen molecule to form ozone, O + O2 → O3.

**Concern:** the ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun. Its depletion, caused mainly by CFCs from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosols, allows more UV to reach the earth, causing skin cancer, damage to the eyes, reduced crop yields and harm to marine organisms. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 froze CFC production to protect it.

qa.q: Explain the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
a: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down the dead bodies of plants and animals and their wastes into simple inorganic substances.
These substances — mineral salts, carbon dioxide and water — go back into the soil and air and are reused by the producers.
They also clean up the environment. Without decomposers nutrients would stay locked in dead matter and the cycling of matter would stop.

qa.q: A village panchayat plans to burn its collected plastic waste in the open. Advise them, giving reasons from what you have studied about ecosystems.
a: Open burning of plastic releases poisonous gases such as hydrogen chloride and dioxins into the air, harming people, animals and crops.
Plastics are non-biodegradable, so if they are buried or dumped they persist in the soil for decades and choke drains and the guts of animals.
Better: segregate waste at source, send recyclable plastic for recycling, compost the biodegradable fraction, and replace single-use plastic with cloth or paper bags.
This keeps harmful chemicals out of the soil and water, so they cannot enter food chains and build up by biological magnification.

qa.q: What is biological magnification? Will the level of magnification be different at different levels of the ecosystem?
a: Biological magnification is the progressive increase in the concentration of non-biodegradable harmful chemicals at successive trophic levels of a food chain.

Yes, the level differs. Because these chemicals are not metabolised or excreted, they pass on to the next level, and the amount of food consumed at each level is large, so the concentration keeps increasing.

**Example:** DDT sprayed on crops is absorbed by plants; grasshoppers eating many plants accumulate more; frogs eating many grasshoppers more still; and hawks at the top accumulate the highest concentration. Human beings, being at the top of many food chains, are among the most affected.

task: Survey your own household waste for three days and sort it into biodegradable and non-biodegradable. Weigh or count each group, then list two things you could refuse or reuse that would remove the largest share of the non-biodegradable waste from the bin.
steps: 1. Identify the level the question is set at: **ecosystem components** (biotic and abiotic), a **food chain or web**, or **waste management**.

2. For a food chain, write the arrow as **'is eaten by'** and place the producer first. If a pesticide or energy question follows, apply the **10 per cent law** at each trophic level and quote biological magnification for harmful chemicals.
3. For depletion or pollution, name the **cause, the mechanism and one remedy** — for example, CFCs break ozone, and the remedy was to phase them out under the Montreal Protocol.
4. Close with the **action** that is asked for: reduce, reuse, recycle (with 'refuse' and 'rethink' if the question wants the full five Rs), and segregate biodegradable from non-biodegradable waste.
